title: Module 12: Getting the Help You Deserve

screens.heading: You are safe here
screens.reassurance: Nothing on this page will contact any company or share your information. You are just reading.
screens.goal: By the end of this module, you will know how to get past chatbots to a real person, navigate language barriers, manage well-meaning family helpers, and spot fake tech support scams.

screens.heading: You deserve good help
body: Getting help with technology — or with a bill, a charge, or a complaint — should not feel like a battle. But it sometimes does. You wait on hold, press endless buttons, and still feel like you did not get what you needed.
This module is about changing that. You have rights as a consumer in Canada. You have resources available to you.
You have the right to ask for help at your own pace, in plain language, until you fully understand. You are allowed to say: 'Please explain that again more slowly.'
screens.tellMeMore: The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) has a Wireless Code and a Television Service Provider Code that give you specific rights with your phone and internet company. You have the right to a clear bill, to cancel without unreasonable penalties, and to have your complaint investigated. Keep these in mind when dealing with a provider.

screens.heading: Getting past chatbots to a real person
body: Most companies now use AI chatbots as the first point of contact. They are often unhelpful for complex problems. To reach a real person faster: say 'agent,' 'representative,' or 'speak to a person' — many automated systems respond to this.

If the chatbot gives you a form to fill out, you can still call the company directly. Look for the phone number on the back of your bill, card, or on the company's official website (not in an email they sent you).
The best times to call: Tuesday to Thursday between 10am and noon local time. Call volumes are lowest then. Mondays are always the worst.
screens.tellMeMore: If you are transferred between departments and have to re-explain your situation each time, start your call by saying: 'I have been transferred twice. Can you note my situation in the file so I do not have to repeat it?' Most agents will do this. Also ask for the agent's name and a reference number at the start — this creates accountability.

screens.heading: Safe remote support — and the fake version
body: Real tech support: your bank, Apple, Microsoft, or a trusted family member can sometimes fix issues on your device remotely. This is safe when YOU initiate the call using a number from the official website.

Fake tech support scam: a pop-up or phone call says your computer has a virus and gives you a number to call. They then ask permission to 'fix' your computer remotely — and steal your data or money instead.
The rule: never allow remote access to your device unless you called the company first using a number you found yourself. Hang up on anyone who calls you unsolicited and asks to access your computer.
screens.tellMeMore: If you have already given someone remote access and suspect it was a scam: disconnect from the internet immediately (turn off Wi-Fi or unplug your router), then call your bank to flag your accounts, and call a trusted family member or local computer repair shop. Change your passwords from a different device.

screens.heading: Managing well-meaning helpers
body: Family and friends often want to help with technology — and sometimes take over instead of teaching. It is completely reasonable to say: 'Please show me how to do it myself, not just do it for me.'
If you feel rushed, say: 'I need a moment to understand this before we move on.' Anyone who genuinely wants to help you will slow down.
You are allowed to write things down, ask questions twice, and decline help when you do not need it. Accepting help does not mean giving up control of your device or your accounts.
screens.tellMeMore: If you ever feel that someone — including a family member — is accessing your device, accounts, or finances without your permission, that is a serious concern. Contact the Seniors Safety Line (Ontario: 1-866-299-1011) or your local police. Elder financial abuse by family members is more common than people realise, and there is confidential help available.

screens.heading: You know how to get the help you deserve
takeaways: Say 'agent' or 'representative' to skip chatbots. Call Tuesday to Thursday, 10am–noon, for shortest wait times.
You have consumer rights in Canada. The CRTC protects you with your phone and internet provider.
Never allow remote access to your device unless you called the company first using their official number.
You can ask anyone helping you to slow down, explain again, and show you how to do it yourself.
Elder financial or technological abuse by family members is real. Help is available at 1-866-299-1011 (Ontario Seniors Safety Line).
screens.confidence: You now know how to get real help — past the chatbots and scripts — and how to protect yourself from fake help designed to take advantage of you.
